name: Zoe Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and lead an electricity company crew that builds and repairs power lines. My two-year technical diploma helps when the fault drawing is messy, and I use AI every day to sort photos of damaged hardware before the truck leaves the yard. I still want an apprentice to point to the crack with their own eyes. The lower pay for this lead work and a savings account that cannot cover a month keep my partner and me talking about retirement as a question rather than a date; our children are grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a modest AI tool already helps me sort repair photos, but the actual line still needs us. A labelled AI photo will not hold a cracked power line crossarm together for the next storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technology does not scare me in this version; our money does. I lead difficult work on a lower-than-usual wage, we have less than a month saved, and few nearby line jobs offer a quick alternative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the lead rota and check each photo label against the pole before ordering parts. Starting with the next pay packet, I would put twenty-five into an emergency account if the household bills are covered, then review it with my partner each payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the ordinary budget, interested in the tool. AI staying mild would not fix the pay gap I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a photo label is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cracked crossarm could be labelled as a loose bracket, and then the crew brings the wrong kit. I would correct the label against the pole tag before submitting the order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if twenty-five is too much on a payday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would skip that transfer and pay food and housing first. My partner and I would not borrow to make a savings target look tidy.

say: I **use** AI for photo sorting, while the crew still repairs physical power lines.
I would **keep** checking labels against pole tags before ordering parts.
think: Our **lower** lead pay and savings below one month make existing bills stressful.
**Few** nearby lineworker jobs limit a quick wage fix.
do: **Keep** lead shifts and verify photo labels at each pole.
**Save** twenty-five from each pay packet when household bills permit.
feel: **Anxious** about current money, interested in modest AI help.
S0.quote: A labelled AI photo will not hold a cracked power line crossarm together for the next storm.
fieldNote: She **uses** AI daily without treating its labels as field truth.
**New** savings come from future pay packets only when ordinary food and housing bills permit, not from moving existing cash.

steps.text: Keep lead shifts and verify AI photo labels against pole tags
Save twenty-five from each pay packet if household bills permit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say stronger AI in buying and booking could keep a crew from waiting for the wrong part, but we should get paid to correct mistakes. A power line fault map needs a paid field correction before its wrong pole becomes someone’s work target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning staff could be cut before lineworkers, and our crew might then inherit rushed callouts. My lower wage and tiny cushion mean even fewer paid hours would reach our household right away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI fault map’s correction controls on a paid shift and compare its suggestions with ten signed repair sheets. In the first year I would bring those errors to our union technology group and ask for paid checking time in the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, but ready to test the tool. I want a chance to improve the work before a bad map becomes a target against us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error would you put first on the union list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would choose a map that points to the wrong side of a switch because the crew would waste time and might use the wrong isolation plan. I would attach the signed repair sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company offers unpaid checking time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would correct a live safety error on the job, but I would refuse a standing unpaid review duty. The union group could ask for the checking hours to be put on the schedule.

say: **AI** fault maps should have paid field correction time.
I would **bring** signed repair evidence to the union technology group.
think: **Planning** jobs may shrink first, while rushed callouts could reduce my own paid hours.
**Thin** savings leave little room for a scheduling mistake.
do: **Learn** AI fault map correction controls on paid shift.
**Compare** ten map suggestions with signed repair sheets.
**Bring** errors to union group for paid checking hours.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours, but willing to test a useful tool.
S1.quote: A power line fault map needs a paid field correction before its wrong pole becomes someone’s work target.
fieldNote: Her **daily** AI fluency makes active error testing plausible, while pay remains nonnegotiable.
She **uses** a union group to protect paid field correction time, not to reject the tool.

steps.text: Learn AI fault map controls during paid shift
Bring ten signed map errors to union technology group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that thinking AI by 2028 could draft every repair plan, and capable line robots around 2031 could take the climb. A line robot should make its first crossarm mistake on a paid trial, not on a street my crew must repair at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty for thinking AI and sixty-three for robots I could still need years of wages. I am skilled enough to test a machine, but our savings below one month and scarce local line jobs mean a lost lead shift lands immediately on food and housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the union to seek paid trial places and a written stop rule. In the first year after 2028 I would learn the robot stop control if the company pays for trial shifts, and I would cancel our paid sports subscription if callout hours actually fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and moving fast, not certain that I will lose the job. I would rather find a machine’s mistake on paid time than let the family pay for an unpaid experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the camera missed a split crossarm or the grip crossed the isolation marker, I would stop it and photograph the site. A clean yard demonstration would not answer that case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner if callouts drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the actual lost pay on two statements, then agree which optional bill goes first. I would not say retirement is impossible without first asking what paid trial or line work remains.

say: **Thinking** AI reaches plans in 2028, with capable line robots following around 2031.
I would **seek** paid field trials and a worker stop rule.
think: **Robot** callouts might shrink while I still need wages at sixty-three.
**Thin** savings and few local jobs make a short paid-hour loss serious.
do: **Ask** union for paid robot trial places and written stop rule.
**Learn** robot stop control after 2028 only on paid trial shifts.
**Cancel** sports subscription only if callout pay actually drops.
feel: **Anxious** about immediate household effects, though actively seeking paid work.
S2.quote: A line robot should make its first crossarm mistake on a paid trial, not on a street my crew must repair at night.
fieldNote: She **expects** a real possibility of lost hours but still sees a paid testing route.
The **spending** cut is conditional on actual lost callout pay, not the scenario alone.

steps.text: Ask union group for paid robot trial places and stop rule
Learn robot stop control on paid trial shifts after 2028
Cancel sports subscription if callout pay drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2031 reaches dispatch when I am sixty-three, and capable robots around 2034 reach line repairs when I am sixty-six. The extra years could let our company train field examiners before a machine works alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be a good examiner because I know what a damaged pole looks like outside the photograph. A field examiner cannot pay the food bill with a certificate and a promised power line job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the company’s examiner course details, paid hours and posted local wage this year. If the course is funded on paid time and a real examiner vacancy covers our living costs, I would enroll before 2031 and apply when posted; until then I would keep leading repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our cash, with a more useful runway than the fast case. A new title only matters if a wage arrives with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must an examiner course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a wrong AI photo label, a wet pole and a damaged crossarm in the same practice job. The trainee should stop the machine before signing anything safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company posts only a lower-paid job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay with the line crew and compare our bills with the actual offer. If the gap is too large, I would ask the union to argue for a proper examiner rate.

say: The **years** to 2034 allow paid field examiner training before robots repair lines.
I would **insist** on real fault practice, not only image review.
think: My **field** skill may transfer, but unpaid study worsens our thin savings.
A **local** examiner post needs pay that covers household costs.
do: **Request** examiner course funding and posted local pay this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if paid course and adequate local vacancy appear.
**Apply** for posted examiner role only if wage covers household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about present cash despite a longer training runway.
S3.quote: A field examiner cannot pay the food bill with a certificate and a promised power line job.
fieldNote: She is **willing** to train, but only with paid hours and an actual adequate vacancy.
Her **strong** field skill and daily AI use do not erase the low-pay household constraint.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if examiner course funded and adequate local vacancy posted
Apply for posted examiner role if wage covers household bills
Keep leading line repairs until suitable paid offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2036 reaches the depot when I am sixty-eight, and capable robots around 2039 reach the pole at seventy-one. I would want my last working years to include paid apprentice lessons on checking machine plans against real hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may be retired by then if income figures and health allow, but less than a month saved today gives me no reason to assume it. If I still need a wage, teaching from the ground could use my diploma without making me climb every storm night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the electricity company this year about paid apprentice teaching hours and check the outside-work rules. If it cannot offer enough hours, I would run two paid weekend diagram sessions for apprentices at the community room only if the company permits it and trainees actually book; I would keep my lead shifts while testing that income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our current savings, even with ten years before the machines. I can draw a power line for an apprentice without betting our last food money on a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge for the weekend sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask each apprentice a small fee for a two-hour lesson and use sketches I already own. If no one books, I would cancel rather than rent a room or print a stack of materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprentices learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would compare a robot plan with a real pole tag and mark the missed hazard. I would insist they explain the physical reason before looking at the screen again.

say: The **long** timeline permits paid apprentice lessons before robots reach lines around 2039.
I would **keep** physical checks in any machine-plan lesson.
think: **Retirement** at sixty-eight is possible, but current savings cannot guarantee it.
**Paid** ground teaching could replace some climbs if I still need wages.
do: **Ask** company about paid apprentice teaching and outside-work rules.
**Run** two paid weekend diagram sessions if company hours are inadequate, employer permits, and apprentices book.
**Keep** crew lead shifts while testing small teaching income.
feel: **Anxious** about current cash, encouraged by a low-cost paid option.
S4.quote: I can draw a power line for an apprentice without betting our last food money on a new machine.
fieldNote: She **explores** a small paid side income without risking capital or assuming students.
**Company** permission and actual apprentice bookings are conditions for the paid sessions; she would cancel rather than risk money on empty seats.

steps.text: Run paid diagram sessions if company hours inadequate, employer permits, apprentices book
Keep electricity company lead shifts while testing teaching income

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable line robots around 2031 could cut lead callouts while our savings still cover less than a month. Paid field trials with stop controls and a real examiner wage would help. I can read an AI fault map every day, but I cannot feed my partner with an unpaid robot test.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask why a lead worker with a diploma is paid near the bottom of the trade. I want the union to keep checking that gap while the company talks about machines. My grown children have their own budgets; they are not my retirement plan.

headlineQuote: I can read an AI fault map every day, but I cannot feed my partner with an unpaid robot test.
portrait: **Zoe** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company crew lead with a two-year technical diploma and daily AI use for fault photos.
**Lower** pay, less than one month saved and few nearby line jobs keep retirement uncertain for her and her partner.
She **uses** union work to seek paid correction and robot trial time while checking machine plans against damaged hardware.
With **more** time she considers a funded field examiner role or small paid apprentice lessons, always keeping household income in view.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring robots around 2031 while her thin savings make lost lead callouts hard to absorb.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** robot trials with stop controls and a real field examiner wage would help her keep earning safely.
